Learning Objectives
Describe the pathophysiology, presentation, and management of acute compartment
syndrome in patients with a tibial shaft fracture.
Describe the acute management of open tibial shaft fractures.
Recognize the indications and contraindications for nonsurgical versus surgical management
of tibial shaft fractures and for intramedullary nailing versus plate fixation.
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of various approaches for the intramedullary
nailing of tibial shaft fractures.
Describe the risk factors and management of infection, malunion, knee pain, malalignment,
and nonunion after a tibial shaft fracture.

Overview
Definition and demographics
Tibial shaft fractures are diaphyseal fractures in the proximal, middle, or distal third of the
tibia.
They are the most common type of long bone fracture, with an incidence of 16.9 per 100,000
per year1 and are associated with considerable short- and long-term morbidity and
substantial medical and economic costs.2
Epidemiology
Tibial shaft fractures have a bimodal incidence.
In older patients, they typically result from low-energy trauma. These fractures account for
4% of all fractures in the Medicare population.
In younger patients, a high-energy mechanism of injury typically is involved.
Isolated fibular shaft fractures are rare and usually result from a direct impact; they also may
be associated with rotational ankle injuries (Maisonneuve fractures).
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The anteromedial crest of the tibia is subcutaneous and composed of dense cortical bone.
The proximal medullary canal is centered laterally.
The fibular shaft is palpable proximally and distally. The fibula is the site of the muscular
attachment for the peroneal musculature and the flexor hallucis longus. It contributes little to
load bearing (15%).
Vascular Anatomy
Patients with a widely displaced tibial shaft fracture may have diminished or absent distal
pulses. Pulse examination should be repeated after fracture reduction. The ankle-brachial
index provides additional insight into the vascular status of the limb.
CT angiography is indicated for patients with asymmetric pulses after closed reduction and/or
an ankle-brachial index lower than 0.903 to rule out a concomitant vascular injury (Figure 1).

Neural Anatomy
Evaluation of a patient with a tibial shaft fracture should involve a detailed neurovascular
examination.
The main nerves of the lower leg include the superficial peroneal nerve, deep peroneal nerve,
sural nerve, saphenous nerve, and tibial nerve, which innervate the muscles of the
compartments in which they run (Figure 2).
Neuropraxias are common, but complete nerve injuries are rare. The neurovascular
examination should be repeated after closed reduction. Paresthesias often improve after
reduction of deformity.

Musculature
The anterior compartment contains the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor
hallucis longus, anterior tibial artery, and deep peroneal nerve.
The lateral compartment contains the peroneus longus and brevis and the superficial peroneal
nerve.
The superficial posterior compartment contains the gastrocnemius-soleus complex, soleus,
popliteus, and plantaris muscles.
The deep posterior compartment contains the tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor
hallucis longus, posterior tibial artery, peroneal artery, and tibial nerve (Figure 2).
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most tibiofibular shaft fractures result from a torsional (indirect) or bending (direct)
mechanism of injury.
Indirect mechanisms of injury result in spiral or long oblique fractures.
Direct mechanisms of injury result in wedge or short oblique fractures (low energy) or
increased comminution (higher energy).

Stress fractures may occur in athletes and military recruits and result from fatigue failure
(Figure 3).

player with an anterior tibial stress fracture. The anterior tibial stress fracture is not visible
on a plain AP radiograph (A); however, the black line (arrow), which represents the anterior
tibial stress fracture, is observed on a plain lateral radiograph (B). C, Magnification of the
lateral radiograph demonstrates the black line (arrow). (Reproduced from Shindle MK, Endo

Risk Factors
In younger patients, risk factors for tibial shaft fractures include the general risk factors of
high-energy trauma (male sex, motorcycle use, etc.)
In older patients, osteoporosis increases the risk for this injury after a low-energy fall.
Associated Injuries
Soft-tissue injury and open fractures
Tibial shaft fractures frequently are associated with considerable soft-tissue injury.
Approximately 24% of these injuries are open,4 and approximately 60% of the open fractures
are Gustilo-Anderson type III.5
Open fractures are associated with higher risks of infection, particularly if administration of
antibiotic prophylaxis is delayed.6
Ankle injuries
Posterior malleolus fractures are observed in 25% to 39% of patients with a spiral fracture of
the distal third of the tibia7,8 Figure 4. Routine CT for distal third fractures help identify these
injuries because they may not be visible on plain radiographs.
Other associated ankle injuries include lateral and medial malleolus fractures and lateral
ligamentous disruptions.

Tibial plateau fractures
Occult extension of a proximal third tibial shaft fracture to the tibial plateau is less common;
however, surgeons should carefully scrutinize preoperative imaging studies for such injury
because nail placement may lead to subsequent displacement.
Ligamentous knee injuries
Ligamentous knee injuries in association with tibial shaft fractures occasionally have been
reported in the literature.9-11
These are difficult to diagnose acutely because of the instability of the fracture.
Proximal tibiofibular joint dislocations
These are observed in approximately 1.5% of patients with a tibial shaft fracture12 and are
more likely to occur if the fibula is intact.13,14
These combined injuries are associated with a higher risk for compartment syndrome, open
fracture, and peroneal nerve injury.12
Injury Classification
Fracture classification
Fractures usually are described based on the pattern (transverse, spiral, oblique, segmental,
comminuted), location (proximal, middle, or distal third), and amount of comminution.
Fractures of the middle third often are further described by location relative to the isthmus.
The Orthopaedic Trauma Association classification system includes type 42A (simple patterns
—spiral, transverse, or oblique), type 42B (wedge), and type 42C (complex, comminuted;
Figure 5).

Soft-tissue classification
The Oestern and Tscherne classification system is used for closed fractures (Table 1).

Mechanics of Fractures
Comminuted fractures are best managed via relative stability to promote secondary bone
healing.

Mechanics of Fractures
Simple fracture patterns (transverse, oblique, spiral) in this location often result in good
outcomes with relative stability constructs (eg, intramedullary nails). Unique mechanical
stability from intramedullary fixation and dynamic loading contribute to good healing
rates. Absolute stability constructs (eg, lag screws and neutralization plating) may be
considered as fracture morphology permits, particularly in more proximal and more
distal patterns.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
The examiner should inspect the limb for gross deformity, angulation, and malrotation.
Palpation for tenderness and swelling also is important. The anterior tibial crest is
subcutaneous, which makes identification of the fracture site easier.
Neurovascular Examination
The examiner should assess for signs and symptoms of impending compartment syndrome.
SEND FEEDBACK

Pain out of proportion to the injury and/or pain on passive stretch of the toes are the most
important signs. Subjective firmness of the compartment is less reliable. Changes in
sensation or pulse examination are late findings.
Compartment syndrome is more common after high-energy trauma.
Continuous intracompartmental monitoring is indicated in patients who are unable to
communicate (eg, the intubated and sedated patient in the intensive care unit).
Compartment release via fasciotomy is indicated if the patient has one or more of the signs
and symptoms already mentioned and less than 30 mm Hg difference (ΔP) exists between the
compartmental pressure and the diastolic pressure.
After the diagnosis of compartment syndrome is made, all four compartments must be
released.
May be done via a single- or double-incision technique (Figure 6).

Figure 6 Illustrations of the lower leg show the single-incision or perifibular approach, which
allows access to all four compartments via a lateral incision. A, The skin incision is made in line
with and directly over the fibula. B, Release of the lateral compartment (2) can be done directly
after identification of the intermuscular septum. Care must be taken to preserve the superficial
peroneal nerve, and the fasciotomy is done 1 cm posterior to the intermuscular septum. C, If the
anterior compartment (1) needs to be released, the skin is retracted anteriorly, and the
fasciotomy is done 1 cm anterior to the intermuscular septum. D, For the fasciotomy of the
superficial posterior compartment (3), the skin is retracted posteriorly for exposure. E, For
fasciotomy of the deep posterior compartment (4), the lateral and superficial posterior
compartments are retracted, and the compartment is reached by following the interosseous
membrane from the posterior aspect of the fibula. (Adapted from Rorabeck CH: A practical
approach to compartment syndromes: III. Management. Instr Course Lect 1984;32:102-113.)
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain radiographs should include a tibia trauma series (AP and lateral views), with dedicated
ankle or knee views if the fracture extends to the surface of the joint. The entire tibia and
fibula must be visualized from knee to ankle.
After any fracture manipulation, post-reduction radiographs should be obtained.
Computed Tomography
CT often is performed to assess for a nondisplaced posterior malleolus fracture and occult
distal intra-articular extension.
Posterior malleolus fractures are observed in patients with spiral patterns.
The Radiographic Investigation of the Distal Extension of Fractures into the Articular Surface
of the Tibia ratio (fracture length over distance to the tibial plafond) is a new screening tool
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:34 AM
AAOS | Tibial Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001190
14/42

for distal intra-articular extension of distal third fractures. CT evaluation is recommended for
fractures with a fracture-to-plafond ratio, also known as the Radiographic Investigation of the
Distal Extension of Fractures into the Articular Surface of the Tibia ratio, higher than
0.617 (Figure 7).
CT also may be used to assess fracture healing or identify nonunion.
Figure 7 AP ankle radiograph demonstrates measurement of the fracture-to-plafond (FTP) ratio.
Line A indicates the fracture length. Line B indicates the distance from the most inferior aspect of
the shaft fracture to the tibial plafond. The FTP ratio = A:B. (Reproduced with permission from
Behlmer RJ, Simske NM, Graf RM, Kliethermes SA, Lang GJ, Whiting PS: Diagnosing fractures of the
distal tibial articular surface in tibia shaft fractures: Is computed tomography always necessary? J
Orthop Trauma 2021;35[9]:485-489.)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI rarely is indicated in the acute assessment of tibial shaft fractures, except in evaluating for
nondisplaced stress fractures, which typically are not detectable on plain radiographs.
MRI may be beneficial in evaluating the extent of the lesion if a possible pathologic fracture is
suspected.
Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:34 AM
AAOS | Tibial Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001190
15/42

Tibial shaft fractures may be managed surgically or nonsurgically depending on the fracture
and the overall condition of the patient.
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management is indicated for low-energy, stable tibial fractures (eg, axially stable
fracture patterns) and virtually all isolated fibular shaft fractures.
Contraindications
Nonsurgical management is contraindicated for open fractures and fractures with an intact
fibula.
Techniques/Procedures
Initial long leg cast immobilization is indicated, followed by functional bracing in a patellar
tendon–bearing brace or cast, with weight bearing as tolerated after 2 to 3 weeks. Cast-
wedging may be used to correct deformity.
Outcomes
Sarmiento et al18 achieved the best results after closed management of tibial shaft fractures,
with a mean shortening of 4.3 mm, a mean angulation less than 6°, and a nonunion rate of
1.1%. Other studies have not been able to reproduce these results; however, their selection
criteria differed.
Surgical Management
Open fractures require prompt antibiotic administration followed by débridement, irrigation,
and fracture stabilization.
Time to antibiotic administration is the most important variable in preventing infection.6,19,20
The effect of time to débridement and irrigation on infection risk is difficult to study because of
multiple confounding variables; however, patients with a type III fracture who receive
appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis are best débrided within 24 hours.21

Antibiotic selection depends on the severity of the injury, with some variability according to
local antibiogram and resistance patterns22 (Table 3).
At the time of surgery, the traumatic wound can be exploited for reduction and provisional or
permanent plate fixation.
Wound closure should be performed if possible, and antibiotic agents should be considered
for 24 hours after definitive wound closure.

Indications
If acceptable reduction parameters cannot be maintained, including less than 50%
displacement, less than 10° of angulation, less than 1 cm of shortening, and less than 10° of
rotational malalignment
Open fractures, fractures with associated compartment syndrome, inherently unstable
fracture patterns (segmental, comminuted, short, displaced) and patients with multiple injuries
(eg, floating knee)
Patients who cannot tolerate prolonged immobilization because of soft-tissue condition
Stress fractures in which nonsurgical management fails

Contraindications
Patients medically unable to tolerate surgical treatment
Techniques/Procedures
Intramedullary nailing
Reamed intramedullary nailing is the preferred treatment option for unstable fracture
patterns because it allows for the use of a larger diameter nail (with larger locking bolts) and
paradoxically results in maintenance of periosteal perfusion. Reamed nailing has been
associated with decreased revision surgery rates compared with unreamed nailing.23 In
addition, with tibial reaming, concern for embolization of the marrow contents is minimal
compared with femoral reaming.
An unreamed intramedullary nail is looser fitting than a reamed nail and is associated with
less cortical necrosis. It also is associated with a higher rate of locking screw breakage than
reamed intramedullary nailing.24
Use of blocking screws, a unicortical plate, a lateral starting point, and intramedullary nailing
in a semi-extended position may help prevent displacement of proximal fractures into flexion
and valgus25 (Figure 8 and 9).

Use of blocking screws and/or fibular plating may help prevent displacement of distal
fractures into valgus (if at the same level as a fibula fracture) or varus (if the fibula is
intact)25 (Figure 10).
Contraindications to intramedullary nailing include a preexisting tibial shaft deformity that
may preclude intramedullary nail passage and a history of previous intramedullary infection.

intramedullary nailing of distal tibia fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[2]:e62-e71.)
Plates and screws
Open plating techniques typically have been associated with wound problems and nonunion.
Newer plate designs and minimally invasive techniques have allowed these implants to play a
role in the management of metadiaphyseal fractures or in tibial shaft fractures in which
intramedullary nailing is not possible (eg, after total knee arthroplasty or tibial plateau
fixation; Figure 11).

Lateral placement may be preferred to anteromedial placement if soft-tissue concerns exist.
Figure 11 Radiographs of the tibia and fibula of a patient with a tibial shaft fracture between
a stemmed, cemented total knee arthroplasty implant and a previous plate and screw
fixation construct for management of a rotational ankle fracture. Preoperative AP (A) and
lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate the injury. Postoperative lateral (C) and AP (D)
radiographs demonstrate management with the use of plates and screws. (Courtesy of Justin
F. Lucas, MD, San Jose, CA.)
External fixation
External fixation has gained popularity in the management of open tibial fractures with soft-
tissue compromise as a damage control measure.
Advantages of definitive external fixation are its low risk and its ability to provide access to
wounds, provide a mechanically stable construct, and allow for radiographic evaluation.
Several types of frame constructs are available, including half-pin monolateral frames, which
are considered safe and violate tissues on one side only; thin, circular wire frames that allow
fixation in metaphyseal bone; and hybrid frames.
Construct stiffness is increased with increased pin diameter, number of pins on either side of
the fracture, rods closer to the bone, and a multiplane construct.
Preoperative Planning
Review the fracture pattern and anticipated difficulties with reduction or implant placement
and ensure all necessary equipment is available.
Reduction can be achieved indirectly (eg, traction, towel bumps, manual manipulation),
percutaneously (eg, pointed reduction clamps, Figure 12), or via open means with or without
provisional fixation (eg, mini-fragment plating; Figure 13).

Proximal and distal fractures may benefit from blocking screws to narrow the effective canal
diameter.
Proximal fractures are more sensitive to imperfect starting points.
Measure the width of the intramedullary canal at the isthmus to predict the nail size that will
be required.

Patient Positioning
Surgical management is performed on a radiolucent table with a bump under the ipsilateral
hip and a ramp of foam or towels (for semi-extended techniques; Figure 14) or a radiolucent
triangle (for flexed infrapatellar techniques)
The surgeon stands on the ipsilateral side of injury, and the image intensifier enters from the
contralateral side (Figure 14).

Surgical Approaches
Approaches for intramedullary nailing include the classic flexed approaches (transtendinous,
paratendinous) and the newer semi-extended approaches (suprapatellar, medial parapatellar,
and lateral parapatellar; Figure 15).

Approaches for open reduction and plate fixation can be anterolateral or anteromedial.
Approach selection depends on the initial fracture deformity and soft-tissue status. In general,
varus failure patterns may benefit from a direct medial plate, whereas valgus patterns benefit
from an anterolateral plate (Figure 17); however, compromised soft tissues may require
deviation from this principle.

The anterolateral approach involves an extensile incision 1 cm lateral to the crest of the tibia,

contouring is more demanding because the plate must be twisted.
Postoperative Management
A splint or soft dressing with or without a boot is applied per surgeon preference. The primary
purpose of this is to prevent an equinus contracture in patients who will not be bearing weight
immediately postoperatively.
Weight bearing may begin as soon as immediately postoperatively in patients with an axially
stable pattern and 6 weeks postoperatively in patients with a highly comminuted, very
proximal, or very distal pattern.
Surgeons should continue to monitor patients for signs and symptoms of compartment
syndrome for 12 to 24 hours after intramedullary nailing.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Proximal fracture malalignment
Avoided via semi-extended nailing, perfect starting points and trajectories (Figure 19).
Percutaneous clamps, blocking screws, and/or provisional mini-fragment plate fixation may
further help avoid this complication (Figures 9, 12 and 13).

Nonunion is defined as a fracture that has lost its capacity to unite.
Delayed union is defined as a fracture that takes longer than expected to unite.
Nonunion and delayed union may result from biologic and mechanical factors.35
The Radiographic Union Scale for Tibia and modified Radiographic Union Scale for Tibia scores
are calculated based on the amount of callus observed on each of the four cortices on AP and
lateral radiographs, with scores of 9 and 11, respectively, indicating healing36 (Table 4).
Management may consist of dynamization, exchange nailing, or bone grafting and should
address the underlying etiology (mechanical or biologic) for the nonunion.

Malunion
A high incidence of valgus and procurvatum deformities is observed in patients with a
proximal third fracture.
Varus malunion leads to ipsilateral ankle pain and stiffness.
Knee Pain
Knee pain was previously reported to occur in as many as 50% of patients after tibial nailing;
however, rates have decreased with the use of semi-extended approaches.
Lateral radiographs should be scrutinized to ensure the nail is not too proud proximally.
Infection
Infection may be superficial or deep and is more common in patients with an open fracture.

Deep infection usually is associated with open fractures (fracture hematoma communication)
and may lead to osteomyelitis.
Malalignment
Malalignment often is associated with late loss of reduction, such as that which may occur with
cast immobilization or external fixation in proximal and distal metaphyseal fractures.
Immediate postoperative malalignment is preventable with careful surgical technique and
awareness of this potential complication, particularly with nailing of proximal or distal tibia
fractures.
Methods to prevent malalignment during tibial nailing include blocking screws, provisional
plating, universal distractors, and fibular plating.
A more lateral proximal entry site should be considered to avoid valgus with a proximal one-
third fracture.
Hardware Malpositioning
Painful hardware may occur because locking bolts and plates usually are placed on the
subcutaneous border of the tibia.
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
To date, thromboprophylaxis has not affected the rate of venous thromboembolism events in
patients with an isolated lower extremity fracture below the knee.37,38
Thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin or similar should be considered in the
context of the injury severity, weight-bearing and immobilization status, patient comorbidities,
and concomitant injuries.39
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Nerve injury, usually affecting the peroneal (most common) or the saphenous nerve, may
occur. The saphenous nerve may be injured during the placement of locking bolts.
An understanding of the anatomy and maintaining tines on bone help avoid inadvertent injury
to the anterior and posterior neurovascular bundles during percutaneous clamp
placement.40,41

Transient deep peroneal nerve palsy affecting the extensor hallucis longus and sensation to
the first dorsal web space occasionally occurs after closed nailing (5%) and typically resolves
over 3 to 4 months.42
Other Complications
Missed compartment syndrome
Failure to identify impending compartment syndrome is the most serious complication after
tibiofibular shaft fractures.
The surgeon should continue to monitor the patient for signs and symptoms of
compartment syndrome for 24 hours postoperatively.
Rehabilitation
After surgical management, weight-bearing status depends on the surgeon preference,
fracture pattern, and implant type. For axially stable fracture patterns with bony contact,
weight bearing as tolerated is allowed. For comminuted fractures, partial–weight bearing is
allowed until radiographic signs of healing are apparent.
Repeat radiographs should be obtained at 6 and 12 weeks postoperatively.
Proximal and distal patterns may benefit from earlier radiographs (2 to 4 weeks
postoperatively) to assess for subsequent fracture displacement.
External fixators should be dynamized before removal to ensure healing and prevent repeat
fracture.
Outcomes
Overall union rate for tibial shaft fractures managed via IM nailing is higher than 85%.23
Multiple studies have shown faster time to union, earlier return to work, and improved knee
function with surgical management compared with nonsurgical management.43-47
In the largest published series on long-term outcomes of tibial shaft fractures, only 45% of
patients were pain-free at final follow-up. Open fracture and delayed union or nonunion are
associated with poorer outcomes. Patients who were injured playing sports had the best
outcomes, whereas patients struck by motor vehicles had the poorest outcomes. Seventy-five
percent of patients returned to their previous level of employment.48

Pearls and Pitfalls
Careful assessment for signs and symptoms of associated sequelae, including compartment
syndrome and vascular injury, is warranted in all tibia fractures.
Timely administration of prophylactic antibiotic agents and surgical débridement help reduce
rates of infection in patients with an open tibia fracture.
Anticipation of deformity in patients with a proximal or distal fracture pattern aids in
restoration of alignment during fixation.
